questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I mainly chose the university because I wanted to go to Paris. This was the only agreement in Paris at my master's degree. I also choose it because the agreement is made with the Sorbonne School of Economics, and I wanted to take courses in economics.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was a bit mixed. The administrative aspects were fairly easy, we received information on where to register and everything. When it comes to information about courses, information was a bit more sparse. I recommend just writing professors directly, if some information about a given course is missing in the course catalogue.

Especially with one course that I took at another university (at Paris School of Economics - the course was part of a shared master's programme with Paris 1), there was no information available, and they could not really help me at the host university. I missed the first class because I had not been informed about it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: After arrival there was an info meeting in the first week, where they explained how to select courses and everything. The selection process itself was easy and I got all the courses I wanted (almost, but only because some schedules were overlapping).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They had said up untill the info meeting that we could choose courses also from other departments than Economics, but then at the meeting they discouraged it because they said they would have no info on exam dates up untill last minute, and if exams where overlapping they would not be able to do anything. Meaning that we would have to come back in the summer (6 months after our Erasmus stay had finished) to take the re-exams. This was a bit annoying, as I would have liked to take some courses at other departments, but did not do it because of this.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It can be very difficult to find accomodation in Paris. I recommend looking (or making a post) in "Padam padam" - a facebook group for Danes in Paris.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Paris is lovely, find your local café and go there many times so people will know you and say hi to you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I don't know about housing available to students. I was not offered anything, but I know they some accomodation via the CROUS organisation. But I think you have to be lucky...

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The course registration happens really late - in september, so after I had arrived in Paris, during the intro week. Up untill that point we had to do our learning agreements and information about courses was not very complete. This was a bit annoying, but perhaps mainly because it stressed me a bit out that we had received no information before the summer started about when and how the registration would take place. It ended up being fine though.

A thing that I found a bit annoying was that the course descriptions were not there for a lot of courses. And for some of the ones where it was, the description was not complete enough. It was difficult to choose courses with the appropriate level and content that suited my academic interests, because of this.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was an info meeting and you could always ask the Erasmus coordinator questions. The help was sufficient when it comes to the administrative part of the registration - but not sufficient when it comes to the content and level of the courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got pretty much all the courses I wanted. The only reason why I did not get all, was because some where overlapping.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
For future students I would recommend just trying to go with the flow - they do not do things as well in advance at Paris 1 as I was used to, but in the end everything worked out.

I also recommend being very proactive in gathering information about the courses. If you find the course descriptions lacking, just write the professors about any questions you might have. I did this towards the end of the process and it was really helpful - I should have done it earlier!

If you are taking Economic History at the PSE, then find information on your own about when it starts - don't wait for Paris 1 to give it to you. Find information on PSE's own website or Thomas Piketty's website.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Varied very much from course to course. And it was a bit difficult for me to assess the level, as I was taking economics courses, but I had not done so much economics before.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level was very different at the different courses (which were at different master's programmes).

I took 4 master level courses and 1 bachelor level course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was generally a bit more old school. For example, I had a course where there was generally no slides or much written materials, you just had to listen and write everything down the professors said. The exams are also written in hand. This made sense of course for the more mathematically oriented exams, but there was also 3-hour exams where you had to make a "problématique" (problemformulering) and answer it with a structured argument essay (this was a bit challenging for me, because it had been a long time since I written that kind of texts in hand). In general, a lot more memorizing stuff than I was used to at KU.

Also some cultural differences: the professor-student relationship is more formal than at KU (en général, il faut toujours vouvoyer les profs, par exemple).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Economic History (at PSE, with Thomas Piketty)

Macroeconomics: Growth (Licence d'économie L3 course)

Techniques quantitatives (at the Sciences économiques et sociales master)

Économétrie appliquée (at the Économie du developpement master and Économie internationale master)

Questions économiques contemporaines (at the Sciences économiques et sociales master)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend the Economic History course to anyone interested in economic and social inequality (and the interplay with ideology and justification) in a historical perspective. It was probably the best course I have ever had.

Économétrie appliquée was a really good course to get a hold of some causal inference econometrics techniques (not that advanced, but interesting course).

Questions économiques contemporaines was also quite interesting with different researchers presenting their topics. It was however very old school (and very French). You French level has to be quite high to follow and to succeed in the exams, I would say.

Techniques quantitatives was a bit too easy - take it only if you want a basic statistics course. A lot of focus on logistic regression and interpretations. I mainly took it to focus on learning to talk about quant. methods in French.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had some medical expenses because I had problems with my eyes. I had to pay directly at the ophtamologist, but hopefully I will get some of it reimbursed.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are bit more expensive than I expected/remembered.

Restaurants are relatively cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I did not sign up for sports, but I took the intro week language course, which was really nice. Met some other erasmus students that I kept having out with during my stay.

I signed up for the language course (Niveau 5 C1 - Méthodologie) and was there the first sessions. I stopped because I found a bit boring - it was more about university methodology (how to take notes, make oral presentations etc.) than an actual French course, I found.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of sports and language courses were available.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you have time, signing up for a sport is probably fun and a great way to meet local students. In general, i found that local students were really nice and up for talking to us erasmus students. Also when it comes to doing things after class, like eating or having some drinks.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
So many things to see and do!

Museums in Paris are generally free if you are under 26 (and a EU citizen).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had lived in Paris before and speak French, so it was quite easy for me.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to people after class or during the breaks. Local students were really nice to include me and invite me to stuff!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mainly that the teaching style was a bit different. More old school, and especially the exams were quite intense (and there were a lot of them).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Life at the cafés and the fact that people talk to each other more in the public space. The culture makes the city feel more vibrant because there is always life everywhere.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
My general impression was that the experience is a lot nicer if your French level is already quite high. There are not that many courses in English to choose from. I met some other erasmus students who struggled quite a bit with the courses in French.

Before the stay: Go with the flow and don't stress out about registration for courses. It does not happen as well in advance as you might be used to/prefer. But they are very flexible when the semester starts, and you can change courses the first 3 weeks of the semester.

Enjoy living in Paris! Try not to let the courses and exams stress you out too much.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne and Sorbonne Université are not the same university. But they share some campus buildings.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Living in Paris and improving my French.

Meeting people from many different countries and making new friends.

Learning some economics.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Two quite intense exam periods (mid-terms and final exams).

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
